questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) What major differences exist between a lava flow and a sill?

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **lava flow** is an **extrusive** igneous body: magma that reaches the surface and spreads out as a sheet of lava. A **sill** is an **intrusive** (hypabyssal) body: a tabular sheet of magma that is injected **between the bedding planes** of the country rock and cools underground. The major differences are:

| Feature | Lava flow | Sill |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Place of emplacement | Erupted onto the Earth's surface (land or sea floor); extrusive | Injected at depth along bedding planes or other planes of weakness; intrusive |
| 2. Rate of cooling and texture | Cools quickly in air or water: **fine-grained or glassy** (basalt, rhyolite), sometimes with a glassy skin | Cools slowly and keeps its heat: **medium-grained** (typically dolerite or microgabbro), with a more uniform texture; the edges are finer (chilled margins) |
| 3. Vesicles | Top (and often base) of the flow is **vesicular or scoriaceous**; vesicles may be filled with minerals (**amygdales**); ropy, blocky (aa) or pillow surfaces | Few or no vesicles, because the overlying rock stops gas escaping; no ropy or blocky surface |
| 4. Contact effects | **Bakes only the rock below it** (the ground over which it flowed); the top is exposed to weathering | **Bakes both the rock above and the rock below** it (two chilled and baked contacts) |
| 5. Age relation with the rocks around it | **Conformable**, the same age as the beds it lies in; younger beds are deposited on its (weathered, reddened or eroded) top, which may carry a soil or **fragments of lava in the overlying sediment** | **Younger than both** the beds above and below; it may include **xenoliths** (pieces of country rock) and may cut across the beds locally (**transgressive** parts) |
| 6. Shape and structures | Thin to thick sheet which thins out in the direction of flow, flow banding, columnar jointing may be present, with a rubbly top and base | Fairly uniform thickness, extensive, often **columnar joints at right angles to the contacts** (the cooling surfaces) |

(Any six correct differences, each stated for both bodies, score full marks.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) With the aid of a diagram describe the Bowen's Reaction Series.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Bowen's Reaction Series** shows the order in which the common silicate minerals crystallise from a cooling basaltic magma, and the way in which the early minerals react with the remaining melt. It has **two branches** which join into one at lower temperature.

**Diagram (to be drawn).** Draw a "Y" shape. Put **temperature** on a vertical arrow, falling downwards from about 1200 °C (high) to about 600 °C (low) (approximate values), and label the branches as follows.

| Level | Discontinuous series (left, ferromagnesian minerals) | Continuous series (right, plagioclase feldspars) |
|---|---|---|
| Top: highest temperature | **Olivine** | **Calcium-rich plagioclase** (anorthite, calcic) |
| Next | **Pyroxene** (augite) | Intermediate plagioclase (labradorite, andesine) |
| Next | **Amphibole** (hornblende) | Plagioclase becoming richer in sodium |
| Lower | **Biotite mica** | **Sodium-rich plagioclase** (albite, sodic) |
| Bottom (the two branches join, lowest temperature) | **Potassium feldspar (orthoclase), then muscovite mica, then quartz** | |

Along the side of the diagram write the rock types that correspond to each level: **ultrabasic and basic** (peridotite, gabbro, basalt) at the top, **intermediate** (diorite, andesite) in the middle, **acid** (granite, rhyolite) at the bottom, and show that the silica content increases and the density decreases downwards.

**Description.**

1. **Discontinuous series.** The minerals change from one to another by an **abrupt change in crystal structure** as the temperature falls: isolated tetrahedra (olivine), single chains (pyroxene), double chains (amphibole), sheets (biotite). Each early mineral **reacts with the melt** and is replaced by the next one (a reaction relationship), so that the rest of the melt is richer in silica.
2. **Continuous series.** The plagioclase feldspar keeps the same framework structure, and its composition changes **gradually and continuously** from calcium-rich to sodium-rich by exchange of $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}} + \mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ for $\mathrm{Na^{+}} + \mathrm{Si^{4+}}$. If cooling is rapid, the reaction is not complete and **zoned crystals** form (calcium-rich cores, sodium-rich rims).
3. **Joining of the two series.** At low temperature the remaining melt, rich in silica, potassium and water, crystallises as **orthoclase, muscovite and finally quartz**, which are the last minerals to form.
4. **Fractional crystallisation.** If the early crystals (olivine, pyroxene, calcium-rich plagioclase) are **removed** from the melt (they settle because they are dense), the magma becomes more silica-rich and a range of rock types (basic to acid) can come from one parent magma (**magmatic differentiation**).
5. **Significance.** Minerals which crystallise **first (at high temperature) are the least stable at the Earth's surface** and weather fastest (olivine), those at the bottom are the most stable (quartz). Minerals that are found together in a rock are those in the same level of the series (for example olivine and calcium-rich plagioclase in gabbro; quartz, orthoclase and mica in granite), and quartz is **never found with olivine**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Describe and account for the formation of any THREE major structures associated with folds.

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Folds are produced by compressive stress, and several secondary structures are formed with them. Three of the major ones are described (the folds themselves, anticlines and synclines, are the primary structures).

**1. Axial planar cleavage (slaty cleavage).** This is a set of closely spaced **parallel planes of splitting** which cuts the folded beds and is **parallel to the axial plane** of the fold, so that it makes an angle with the bedding that changes round the fold (bedding and cleavage are nearly parallel on the limbs and at a large angle in the hinge). *Formation:* when fine-grained rocks (shale, mudstone) are folded under compression, the platy minerals (clay minerals, mica, chlorite) are **rotated and recrystallised with their flat faces at right angles to the greatest compressive stress**, and the rock is shortened and flattened in that direction. The cleavage is therefore perpendicular to the maximum compression and parallel to the axial plane. It is best developed in slate.

**2. Joints.** These are **fractures along which no movement has taken place**, found in the fold hinge and limbs. *Formation:* in the outer arc of the hinge of a fold, the beds are stretched (**tension**) and break to give **tension (radial) joints** which open at right angles to the bedding and are fan-shaped. **Cross joints** (parallel to the dip) and **longitudinal joints** (parallel to the strike and fold axis) are produced by tension and compression during folding. They are filled by veins of quartz or calcite and can produce **saddle reefs** or ore deposits, and the joints control the drainage and the weathering of the rocks.

**3. Faults (thrust faults and reverse faults).** *Formation:* when compression continues after the folding, the rocks which are strong (brittle) can no longer fold and **break**. The limb of an overturned (recumbent) fold is thinned, then sheared along a **thrust fault** which moves the upper block over the lower one, and the rock is shortened in both folding and faulting. Smaller faults, **bedding-plane (flexural) slip faults** with **slickensides**, are formed on the limbs of the folds where one bed slips over another, like a pack of cards bent in the hand. Thrusts are very common in mountain belts (fold-and-thrust belts).

(Other correct structures: **boudinage and mullions**, **saddle reefs**, **tear faults**, **slickensides** and **dome and basin structures**. A neat labelled sketch of an anticline with the axial plane, the cleavage, the joints and a thrust is credited.)
